extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and policymakers interested in peer review and Open Science
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic-review-derived taxonomy and definitions of the distinct traits/configurations commonly called 'open peer review', plus the problems in traditional peer review these traits aim to address. Useful for anyone designing, evaluating, or researching peer review models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review usually performs two distinct functions: (1) technical evaluation of the validity or soundness of a work in its methodology, analysis and argumentation (answering the question 'is it good scholarship?'), and (2) assisting editorial selection by assessing the novelty or expected impact of a work ('is it exciting, innovative or important scholarship?', 'is it right for this journal, conference or funding call?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two functions need not be entwined; some journals (e.g., PLOS ONE, PeerJ) ask reviewers to focus only on technical soundness. When evaluating or designing peer review systems, explicitly decide which function(s) the process is meant to serve, as different OPR traits target different functions and problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliability and inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional peer review is reliant upon the vagaries of human judgement; the objectivity, reliability, and consistency of peer review are subject to question, with studies showing weak inter-reviewer agreement and reviewers often failing to detect major methodological failings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion highlights the need for review models or interventions that improve consistency and error-detection. Evidence (e.g., Kravitz et al., Peters & Ceci) should be considered when claiming that any model improves reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can cause long delays from submission to publication (often exceeding one year) and entails substantial global cost in reviewers' time; repeated review cycles across journals amplify time and cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate review models for their impact on time-to-publication and total resource costs; models that decouple review from publication or use preprints may reduce delay and duplicate reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of accountability and risks of subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'black-box' nature of traditional peer review allows reviewers, editors, and authors to potentially subvert the process (e.g., editors shaping outcomes, reviewers concealing conflicts, reviewers stealing ideas, authors gaming reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a review model increases transparency and accountability (e.g., by revealing identities or publishing reports) and weigh risks (e.g., retaliation, strategic behaviour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and publication biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may be subject to biases on the grounds of gender, nationality, institutional affiliation, language, discipline, and there is publication bias favoring positive results and novelty over replications and null results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging peer review systems, consider their ability to mitigate bias (e.g., double-blind procedures) versus the risk of introducing new biases (e.g., open identities may advantage senior scholars). Empirical evidence should be used to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of incentives for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional peer review offers little incentive for reviewers: work is generally unpaid and anonymous contributions are not publicly recognized or rewarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a model provides recognition or credit (e.g., published review reports, signed reviews, ORCID integration) that could serve as incentives and impact reviewer recruitment and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wastefulness (loss of useful review material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer comments, behind-the-scenes discussions, and reviewer disagreements often contain useful information for readers and for scholarly training, yet under traditional models this information is largely hidden and wasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether publishing review reports or otherwise exposing review materials increases reuse, pedagogical value, and community knowledge, and balance this against confidentiality or legal/privacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers are aware of each other’s identity (also termed signed peer review or unblinded review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purported benefits: increased accountability, reviewer credit, potential increase in review quality, clearer conflicts of interest. Risks: self-censorship, poorer candour in reviews. Evidence is mixed and limited (mostly from medicine); implementers should monitor refusal rates, review thoroughness, and disciplinary norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Review reports (either full reports or summaries) are published alongside the relevant article (often, but not always, with reviewer names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: transparency, accountability, reuse of reviews, incentives for reviewers, pedagogical value. Empirical findings: associated with higher reviewer refusal rates and longer review times but no clear effect on review quality in some studies (e.g., van Rooyen et al.). Consider publisher practices (some publish reports anonymously).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider community is able to contribute to the review process (crowdsourced/community/public review), either anonymously or with credentials; may complement solicited peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to reduce editorial selection biases and potentially improve reliability by increasing reviewer numbers. Criticisms include questions about commenters' qualifications and incentives. Models should consider gating (e.g., credential requirements) and scale: some modelling suggests public reviewer accuracy may exceed small expert panels if participation is sufficiently large (e.g., >50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct reciprocal discussion between author(s) and reviewers, and/or between reviewers, is allowed and encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to enable clarifying dialogue, quicker resolution of issues, and collaborative improvement of manuscripts. Consider structure (moderated vs free), timing (pre/post decision), and potential for power-dynamics or conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open pre-review manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts are made immediately available (e.g., via pre-print servers like arXiv) in advance of any formal peer review procedures (the author uses the term 'open pre-review manuscripts' to denote making manuscripts openly available prior to formal review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: accelerates dissemination, allows early community feedback, can enable real-time tracking of review/commentary. Terminology varies (preprints, posting before formal review); designers should be explicit about versioning, moderation, and how preprint comments feed into formal decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open final-version commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing or commenting on final 'version of record' publications is enabled (post-publication commenting on the published article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows ongoing critique and update of the record; typically less common in definitions of OPR. Evaluate moderation policies, integration with the record (do comments lead to corrections/retractions?), and discoverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open platforms ("decoupled review")
rubrics_metrics.description: Review is facilitated by an organizational entity different from the venue of publication (peer review services or platforms decoupled from journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decoupling can enable transferability of reviews, independent review services, and alternative workflows. It is a fringe/rare trait in OPR definitions; consider interoperability, incentives for uptake, and how platform-mediated reviews are trusted by publication venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPR as an umbrella term / configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review is proposed as an umbrella term for a number of overlapping ways that peer review models can be adapted in line with Open Science aims; the literature shows 22 distinct configurations of seven traits, meaning different definitions combine these traits in many ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using 'OPR', specify which trait(s)/configuration are meant (e.g., open identities + open reports vs open participation alone). Recognize core/periphery: open identities and open reports are most prevalent in definitions (present in the majority of sources), while other traits are more peripheral.
